disease_info: Bulimia nervosa is characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors (such as self-induced vomiting, laxative misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise) aimed at preventing weight gain. Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body weight and shape, but individuals are typically within a normal or above-normal weight range, distinguishing it from classic presentations of anorexia nervosa. The disorder often emerges in adolescence or young adulthood but can present or recur later in life, frequently in the context of interpersonal stress, role changes, or weight-focused environments. The course may be chronic or episodic, with shame and secrecy often delaying help-seeking until medical complications, worsening mood, or functional impairment become difficult to hide.

narrative.stressor: About six months ago, Agustín moved out of the apartment he shared with his wife after a drawn-out separation that he describes as "cordial on the surface, but tearing me up underneath." Living alone for the first time in years, he fell out of the shared routines that had structured his days—family dinners, weekend soccer games together, and meal prepping—replacing them with irregular shifts at the rescue center, late-night guitar jams, and solitary cooking sessions that became increasingly emotionally charged. Around the same time, friends and family began commenting on how "lean" he looked, and he started tracking his weight and food intake with the same meticulousness he used in his animal observations, tying his sense of control and attractiveness post-separation to his body size. Over the past five months, what started as "tightening up" his diet after the breakup escalated into cycles of secret overeating followed by drastic measures to avoid weight gain, and he finally sought psychiatric help after noticing how preoccupied he had become with his weight and how guilty and anxious he felt after eating with friends or at Cuban cultural events centered around food.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel like how I look and what I weigh is the only thing that matters about me now, and it’s starting to take over my life around food.

narrative.stressor: Lucy was promoted informally to a lead tech role when her shop started taking on more hybrid and EV work, which meant longer hours, heavier responsibility, and a younger crew looking to her as the example of what a "tough, no-nonsense" mechanic should be. As the workload grew and breaks became more rushed, she found herself grabbing quick, high-calorie meals between jobs and then feeling ashamed when she saw herself in the reflective glass of the service bay next to the slimmer younger techs and the fitness-focused customers. In an effort to "get back in shape" and prove she could keep up physically, she began swinging between eating large amounts of food after stressful shifts and then forcing herself to get rid of it so the weight "wouldn’t stick," a pattern that intensified over the last five months as the shop entered its busiest season. She finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after an embarrassing episode where she had to excuse herself repeatedly during a church potluck, and her pastor’s wife gently asked if she was okay because she seemed "worn down" and was disappearing to the restroom right after eating.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve gotten into this habit of making myself throw up after I eat, and I can’t seem to stop doing it even though I know it’s not right.

narrative.stressor: Over the past year, Maurice has been transitioning into more of a supervisory role at his firm while also thinking seriously about retirement planning, which has stirred up worries about aging, health, and "letting myself go" physically. When his primary care doctor mentioned elevated blood pressure and suggested watching his weight at his last checkup, he began to scrutinize his eating more intensely, feeling conflicted between his love of rich Southern and Haitian cooking and the pressure to "tighten up" for his health. In the last five months, periods of loneliness in the evenings—after his wife fell asleep early or when he skipped church events to do paperwork at home—turned into episodes where he would eat far more than he intended while reading or watching games, followed by deep regret and increasingly rigid attempts the next day to "make up for it." He decided to seek psychiatric care after noticing these eating episodes were becoming more frequent and that, despite his meticulous nature, he felt oddly unable to control himself once he started eating, which frightened him given how carefully he manages every other part of his life.
narrative.chief_complaint: Once I start eating in the evenings, it feels like I can’t stop myself, no matter how much I tell myself I should.
